speaker_role: independent counselor (Ethan Sawyer, College Essay Guy) — course preview/promotional module
commercial_incentive: This is an explicit preview/sample of a paid course module; promotes the full paid course while giving substantial free content
key_insights: Reiterates strong-verb strategy for activity descriptions, contrasting generic verbs ('worked,' 'helping') with more specific ones ('organized,' 'sterilized,' 'prescribed') that convey a clearer sense of role and responsibility.

Advises varying verbs across a single entry so each one adds distinct information rather than restating the same idea (e.g., 'instructing, helping, teaching' all overlap — replace with two verbs that each cover a different aspect).

Recommends quantifying impact wherever possible — naming how many people were helped, how much money was raised, and for what specific purpose, rather than vague claims like 'raised money for children in Africa.'

If a student's role was simply 'member' or 'participant,' advises just listing the activity name rather than repeating a low-status role label, since students don't need to over-explain lack of leadership.

Notes the Common App has an 'additional info' section that can be used selectively (for 3-4 key activities, not all of them) to expand on especially strong or complex accomplishments beyond the 150-character limit.

Contrasts a 'really good' activities list (solid, clear, well-described but ordinary achievements) against an 'amazing' one (extraordinary, verifiable achievements like a patent, a Carnegie Hall performance, or a national ranking) — arguing most students should aim to maximize the quality of description for what they actually have, since extraordinary achievement itself can't be manufactured through writing alone.

Suggests some non-obvious things can count as legitimate 'activities': self-taught coding via online courses, music composition, or training pets — as long as the student explains their personal significance and what was learned.

Repeats a real cautionary anecdote (same story referenced in a related video by the same creator) about a student who fabricated a club officer title and a trip, was reported by inconsistencies discovered by other schools, and was ultimately rejected and required to send an apology letter.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Common App activity descriptions are capped at 150 characters (per speaker).
notable_or_distinctive: The explicit 'really good vs. amazing' side-by-side comparison of real (anonymized) student activity lists — including a genuinely extraordinary example (a granted US patent, Carnegie Hall performance, published video game) — gives a concrete calibration point for what 'exceptional' actually looks like versus merely well-written.
reliability_notes: This is a promotional preview of a paid course module, so it's designed partly to sell the full product, though the content given is substantive and non-salesy in tone; the 'amazing' example list is an outlier/exceptional case and shouldn't be treated as a typical bar to clear.
